Candidate portal

Mock virtual onsite

Three 60-minute technical sessions in the style of a software engineering virtual onsite. Your interviewer releases each stage with a code.

Overview Pre-work Session 1: Integration Locked Session 2: AI programming Locked Session 3: Bug squash Locked After the sessions

How this works

Read this page now, do the pre-work before interview day, and keep the portal open during every session.

  1. Before the day. Open Pre-work, download the environment check and run it. It takes about 15 minutes and removes most of the things that can go wrong.

  2. At the start of each session. Your interviewer gives you a short code. Type it into the session's page here. That unlocks the starter repository and the problem statement.

  3. During Session 2. The problem comes in parts. Each time you finish a part, your interviewer gives you the code for the next one.

The three sessions

SessionLengthWhat you doTools
1. Integration 60 min Add features to an existing codebase that talks to an HTTP API, working from a written spec and API documentation. Your own editor. Documentation and web search are fine. No AI of any kind.
2. AI-enabled programming exercise 60 min: about 10 to settle in, 45 to solve, 5 to wrap up Solve a multi-part programming problem. You see one part at a time. Your own editor with one built-in AI agent, which you are expected to use. No other AI tools.
3. Bug squash 60 min Some tests of a real open-source Python library fail. Find out why and fix the library. You have probably never read its code. Your own editor and debugger. Documentation and web search are fine. No AI of any kind.

In every session you share your screen, think out loud, and can ask your interviewer anything, the way you would ask a teammate. A full new-grad loop has all three sessions; an intern loop has the first two.

What interviewers look for

IntegrationAI-enabled programming exerciseBug squash
Helping yourself: finding your way in unfamiliar code and documentationArchitecture: you set the structure and the constraints, and steer the agent to themTooling: how well you use your debugger, editor and test runner
Abstractions and the code you writeCritical oversight: you read what the agent produces and catch what is wrong or over-builtUnderstanding the code: you can say what the code around the bug does
Correctness, testing and debugging, including not breaking what already worksCorrectness and debugging: good test cases, systematic troubleshooting, working without the agent when it missesForward progress: a strategy, with a hypothesis stated before each check
Interaction and collaborationInteraction and collaborationInteraction and collaboration

No session expects you to finish everything. Careful, tested, well-explained progress counts for more than raw speed. Session 2 ends with the question "How do you know this is correct?" In Session 3 a bug found by luck counts for less than a clear method, and you can pass without finding every bug.

Have ready on the day

  • Python 3.9 or newer and the editor you are fastest in.
  • For Session 2: an AI coding agent inside that editor, signed in, with quota to spare.
  • For Sessions 1 and 3: AI completions switched off in that editor.
  • For Session 3: a debugger you are fluent with, or a decision to debug with print statements.
  • A video call with screen sharing, and this portal in a browser tab.

Pre-work

About 15 minutes, a day or two before the interview. Real onsites allow only a few minutes for setup, so the time to find a broken environment is now.

1. Download and run the environment check

Unzip it, open a terminal in the folder, then:

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate            # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
python check_env.py

Every line should start with [ ok ]. Fix anything marked [FAIL].

2. Rehearse with your AI coding agent

Session 2 is solved together with an agent that lives in your editor: Cursor, VS Code with GitHub Copilot in agent mode, Windsurf, or a command-line agent such as Claude Code, Codex or Gemini CLI running in the editor's terminal. Choose one and use only that one.

Open the environment check folder in that editor and follow step 2 of its README.md: a short warm-up in which the agent makes a set of failing tests pass while you review its work.

You are ready when you can do these without searching through menus:

  • point the agent at files, and let it edit files and run commands;
  • see exactly what it changed, then accept or reject the change;
  • stop it when it heads in the wrong direction;
  • run the tests yourself from the terminal.

3. Rehearse your debugger

Session 3 is about tracking down bugs in code you have not read before. In the environment check folder, run the warm-up tests under a debugger:

python -m pytest warmup -x --pdb     # stops in pdb at the first failure

Or set a breakpoint in warmup/text_stats.py in your editor and run one test in debug mode. You are ready when you can set a breakpoint, step over, into and out, inspect variables, and move up and down the call stack. Print statements are fine too: decide beforehand which you will use.

4. Check your screen share

  • Share the whole editor window: code, terminal and the agent panel.
  • Raise the font size until code is readable over video.
  • Silence notifications and close what should not be on screen.

Session 1: Integration

60 minutes. You extend an existing Python codebase that talks to an HTTP API. No AI tools in this session.

The starter repository and the spec are locked until the session starts.

Start here

  1. Download the starter repository, unzip it and open the folder in your editor.

  2. Turn AI completions off, then share your whole editor window.

  3. Follow Setup in README.md. It is the same text as the spec below.

Session 2: AI-enabled programming exercise

60 minutes: about 10 to settle in, 45 to solve, 5 to wrap up. Use your editor's AI agent throughout, and keep it visible in your screen share.

Start here

  1. Download the starter repository, unzip it and open the folder in the editor that has your AI agent.

  2. Share your whole editor window, including the agent panel.

  3. Follow Setup in README.md. Part 1 below is also in the repository as PROBLEM.md.

When a new part unlocks you can copy it as Markdown, or download it, and save it in the repository so that your agent can read it.

All four parts are unlocked. Most people do not finish all of them in 45 minutes.

Session 3: Bug squash

60 minutes. A real open-source library, a few failing tests, and you find out why. No AI tools in this session.

The repository and the instructions are locked until the session starts.

Start here

  1. Download the repository, unzip it and open the folder in your editor.

  2. Turn AI completions off, then share your whole editor window, terminal included.

  3. Follow Setup in BUGSQUASH.md. It is the same text as below.

After the sessions

When a session is over, your interviewer may give you one more code. For Sessions 1 and 2 it releases the verification suite: the tests your solution is checked against. For Session 3 it releases the debrief notes: where each bug was and how to get to it.
